passage: The college dance club was picking new coordinators in a small seminar room in Pune. Zeenat sat beside Dilnaz, the club president, taking notes. The first candidate, Rohit, walked in with a big smile, made everyone laugh within a minute and praised the club's last show. Dilnaz gave him five out of five for planning, budgeting and teamwork. Zeenat looked at her own notes: asked about budgets, Rohit had said, "I'll figure it out." The next candidate, quiet and nervous, had walked through a full budget from last year's fest. Dilnaz gave her threes. Zeenat leaned over. "Can we score each skill one at a time, using what they actually said?"

qa.q: What did Rohit say when asked about budgets?
qa.a: Rohit had said, "I'll figure it out."

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz give Rohit five out of five for budgeting?
qa.a: His warmth and humour made a strong first impression that spilled over into every skill, even ones he showed no evidence for.

qa.q: Why does Zeenat's suggestion help?
qa.a: Scoring each skill separately, using what candidates actually said, stops one charming minute from lifting every rating.

qa.q: How might the quiet candidate feel on seeing her threes next to Rohit's fives?
qa.a: She would likely feel it was unfair, since she gave a full budget example while he gave none.

grounding: Shows a student noticing an interviewer rate a charming candidate high on every skill and suggesting each skill be scored separately.

passage:
"Wasn't he wonderful?" Manjula said, closing the door after the last candidate. "Such confidence. Great communicator, great analyst, great leader. Tens everywhere."
Devika glanced at her notes. "He was very charming. But in the case question, he never got to a number."
"He explained his thinking beautifully."
"He did. So, ten for communication?"
"Obviously."
"And analysis? The other candidate solved the case."
Manjula hesitated. "Well... maybe a six for analysis."
"Leadership?"
"He didn't really give an example, did he?"
"No."
Manjula crossed out a ten. "Funny. When I think of him all at once, he's a ten. One box at a time, he isn't."

qa.q: What did the candidate fail to do in the case question?
qa.a: He never got to a number in the case question.

qa.q: What does Manjula's line "When I think of him all at once, he's a ten" reveal?
qa.a: It reveals that Manjula's warm overall impression was lifting every score, and only breaking it into boxes showed the gaps.

qa.q: Which of Devika's moves made the difference?
qa.a: Asking about one skill at a time, using the notes, let Manjula judge each area on evidence instead of on the glow of confidence.

qa.q: How might the other candidate, who solved the case, be affected by Devika's questions?
qa.a: That candidate's analysis is more likely to be scored fairly now, instead of being overshadowed by a charming rival.

grounding: Shows a young colleague seeing an interviewer rate a charming candidate high across the board and weakening the halo by going skill by skill.

passage: Last summer, as a student volunteer at a startup's hiring day, I learned how one smile can colour everything. I'm Disha. I sat beside Anand, the engineering manager, while he interviewed applicants. One candidate had a warm handshake, a great story about a trek and an easy laugh. By the end, Anand had marked her "excellent" in coding, testing and teamwork. But I had watched her coding round: she stalled on the second problem. Nervously, I asked if we could fill the score sheet one column at a time, with an example beside each. He paused, then agreed. Her coding went down to "fair". I still think about how easily I'd have given her "excellent" too.

qa.q: Where did the candidate stall?
qa.a: She stalled on the second problem in her coding round.

qa.q: Why did Anand mark the candidate excellent in coding?
qa.a: Her warm handshake, good story and easy laugh created a glow that spread to every skill, including one where she struggled.

qa.q: Why did the column-by-column score sheet work?
qa.a: Filling in one skill at a time with an example beside it forced each rating to rest on what actually happened, weakening the first impression's glow.

qa.q: How might other candidates be affected by Disha speaking up?
qa.a: Candidates without a charming story but with strong coding would now be compared fairly on the skills that matter.

grounding: Shows a young volunteer noticing an interviewer rate a charming candidate high in every skill and suggesting scoring each skill separately.

passage:
Mock interview day, placement cell, Thursday. Note by Trisha, final-year coordinator.
I sat in on the panel with Ojas, an alumnus volunteering as interviewer. The third candidate, a second-year named Wasim, walked in smiling, joked about the broken fan, and had Ojas laughing within a minute. His answer on the coding question was vague, and he admitted he hadn't finished his project. Ojas still gave him 9 for communication, 9 for technical skills, 9 for teamwork. I had written 8, 5 and 6.
I didn't want to embarrass Ojas, so at the break I asked, "Could we try the next five with one line per skill, scored right after that question, before the overall score?" He agreed.
The next candidate was also very likeable. This time Ojas scored her 8 for communication and 4 for technical. He looked at the sheet and said, "Huh. I'd have given her all nines."
Next step: I'll ask the placement cell to use the split sheet for every panel.

qa.q: What scores did Ojas give Wasim for communication, technical skills and teamwork?
qa.a: He gave him 9 for communication, 9 for technical skills and 9 for teamwork.

qa.q: Why did giving Wasim nines across the board likely feel fair to Ojas at the time?
qa.a: Wasim was warm and funny and had Ojas laughing within a minute, so that good feeling spread over everything and made the vague answers seem less important.

qa.q: What change did Trisha suggest, and what showed it helped?
qa.a: Trisha asked to score one line per skill right after each question, before the overall score, and Ojas then gave the next likeable candidate 8 for communication and 4 for technical.

qa.q: If Trisha had said nothing, how might the split sheets and panels have turned out for other students?
qa.a: Charming students might keep getting high marks in skills they had not shown, while quieter candidates with strong answers could be ranked lower than they deserve.

grounding: It shows a peer noticing an interviewer rate a charming candidate highly across every skill, and separate per-skill scoring reducing the effect.

passage:
Sat, after the bookshop closed
Usha asked me to sit in on today's interviews for the weekend assistant job. It's the first time she's let me help with hiring, so I kept quiet and took notes.
The second person, Farhan, was lovely. Great smile, remembered my name, talked about his favourite novels for ten minutes. Usha was glowing afterwards. "Reliable, organised, great with customers. Perfect."
But he'd said he can only do alternate weekends, and when she asked him to find a book on the shelf by its code, he couldn't. I wrote that down.
I didn't say much today. I just showed her my notes. She was quiet for a moment and said, "Hm. I didn't hear the weekends part at all."
Tomorrow I'm making a little sheet: one box for reliability, one for shelving, one for customers, filled in straight after each question. Next interview, we score the boxes first, overall last.
Vishal

qa.q: What did Farhan say about which weekends he could work?
qa.a: He said he can only do alternate weekends.

qa.q: Why might Usha have missed the weekends detail, according to what Vishal saw?
qa.a: Farhan's smile and warm talk made her feel good about him overall, so his likeability seemed to cover reliability and organisation too, and the weekends part slipped past her.

qa.q: What small step does Vishal plan for the next interview?
qa.a: Vishal is making a sheet with one box each for reliability, shelving and customers, filled in right after each question, with the overall score last.

qa.q: How might Vishal feel when Usha admits missing the weekends part?
qa.a: Vishal probably feels relieved and encouraged, since quietly showing the notes worked, which is why Vishal plans the scoring sheet for the next interview.

grounding: It shows a young peer noticing an interviewer's warm first impression lift every rating, and planning separate per-skill scoring to weaken it.
